pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Simple tests and experiments

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to perform simple tests, and to use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions. 'Comparative and fair testing' is one of the five named enquiry types; at KS1 this begins as simple tests where the child changes one thing and watches what happens.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, grades K–2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1], and make observations and/or measurements; investigations should be based on fair tests, in which one variable is changed while others are kept the same. Doing a simple test to answer a question is the entry investigation practice.

- **Operational details:** The child carries out a genuine simple test to answer a question — changing ONE thing at a time (which ramp angle makes the car go furthest? which material keeps the teddy driest?), observing and describing what happens, and then using that result to suggest an answer to the original question. The key procedural seed is 'change one thing, watch what happens, then say what you found out': the test is deliberately set up to answer a question, not just to play, and the answer is grounded in what was observed rather than what the child already believed. This is the first, informal version of fair testing and it feeds directly into recording data and, later, controlled variables.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). This is where a question becomes an ACTION: you don't just wonder or look it up, you set up a little test and let the result answer you. Success = plans and does a simple test that changes one thing, observes and describes the result, and uses that result to suggest an answer to the starting question.
bestPractices: Start from a real question the child cares about, so the test has an obvious purpose (answering it), not just an activity to complete.
Establish 'change one thing, keep the rest the same' informally, even before the vocabulary of variables, by doing side-by-side comparisons.
Insist the answer comes from what was OBSERVED ('the car went furthest from the high ramp') rather than from prior belief.
Use predict–do–observe: let children say what they think will happen, then test, so results can surprise and inform them.
Keep tests concrete and physical (ramps, materials, floating/sinking) so cause and result are directly visible.
Model the loop explicitly: question → test → observe → 'so my answer is…', naming each step.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side comparison set-up (same except for the one thing being changed)
Predict-then-test card (what I think → what happened)
Simple result record (drawing/tally of what was observed)
'One thing changed' highlight showing what was kept the same
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a test is just playing or 'having a go', not a way to answer a question.
Changing several things at once, so it's unclear what caused the result.
Deciding the answer from what you already believed rather than from what you observed.
Believing the 'right' result is the one that matches your prediction.
Not connecting the result back to the original question (doing the test but not drawing the answer).
Thinking you only need to do a test once and can't repeat or check it.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–7 learning to perform simple fair tests: turn a real question into a doing-and-observing loop — change ONE thing, keep the rest the same, watch and describe what happens, then use that observed result to answer the starting question. Because the objective is to PERFORM a test, the enacted test the child runs (on-screen or with real ramps/materials) is the core; tap-to-reveal scenes, planning talk, and a short review act as primers or checks around the actual doing.

activities.title: Test Bench: which ramp sends the car furthest?
feedback: When the child changes only ramp height and reads the flags: 'You changed just one thing — the height — so you can SEE which ramp wins, not just guess.'
If the child changes two things at once (e.g. swaps the car and raises the ramp): 'Change just one thing, or we won't know what made the difference.'
If the child names the guess instead of the result: 'Show me which flag went furthest — let's answer from what really happened.'
activities.rationale: KS1 Working Scientifically (performing simple tests) and NGSS SEP 3 (K–2: with guidance, plan and conduct simple investigations and make observations to compare) both start investigation with simple, guided tests where the answer comes from observation. Changing one thing while keeping the rest the same is an informal start here; formal fair tests with controlled variables are stressed more in later grades (e.g. KS2, NGSS 3–5). An enacted test — on screen with a height slider, GO button and measuring strip, or with real ramps — lets the child generate and read off a result, which is the heart of the testing practice rather than only recognising it. A visible measured outcome (flag position on a strip) and a gentle prompt against changing two things make the cause-and-result link concrete; these are example mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to perform simple tests and to use observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions; comparative and fair testing is one of the five named enquiry types.
NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) K–2 has students, with guidance, plan and conduct investigations based on fair tests, changing one variable while keeping others the same.
learnerActions: Start from a real question the child cares about, e.g. 'Which ramp makes the toy car roll the FURTHEST?'
Say your guess first (predict), then set the ramp low, release the car, and mark where it stops with a flag.
Change ONE thing — raise the ramp height — release the same car again, and mark where it stops with a new flag.
Compare the flags and finish the sentence 'The car goes furthest when the ramp is…' by choosing the answer the flags actually show.
If tempted to also swap the car or the floor surface at the same time, change only one thing so you can tell what made the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A test is a way to make the world answer your question: when I change one thing and watch, the result shows me the answer instead of me just guessing.

activities.title: Which surface lets the car roll furthest? (real materials)
feedback: If the child gives the car a harder push or a different start on a favourite surface: 'Did each surface get a fair go? What did you change? Let's release it from the same spot each time.'
If the child names the surface they predicted rather than the one that actually won: 'Show me which one really went furthest — let's answer from what we saw.'
If the child narrates the fun ('it went really fast!') without concluding: 'So, which surface lets the car roll the furthest?'
activities.rationale: At 5–7 this PROCEDURAL objective requires an enacted test the child actually runs and observes (real or on-screen); here the concrete, hands-on set-up of real ramps and surfaces (and floating/sinking in related tests) makes cause and result directly visible. Releasing rather than pushing and keeping the start point fixed is the informal seed of controlled variables. The answer must be tied back to the observed result, closing the question→test→observe→answer loop.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to perform simple tests and to use observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions; comparative and fair testing is one of the five named enquiry types.
NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) K–2 has students, with guidance, plan and conduct investigations based on fair tests, changing one variable while keeping others the same.
learnerActions: Set out a ramp, a toy car and three floor surfaces at the bottom of the ramp — carpet, smooth wood, bubble wrap — with the question 'which surface lets the car roll the furthest?'
Release (don't push) the same car from the same spot on the same ramp onto each surface in turn, changing only the surface.
Watch and describe how far the car goes each time (mark or tally the distance).
Keep everything else the same each time so each surface gets a fair go.
Finish by answering the question directly from your own marks, e.g. 'the [surface], because the car rolled furthest on it' (add 'every time' only if you repeated the runs and it won each time).
activities.intendedInsight: To compare fairly, release the same car from the same start point the same way (no extra push) and change only the surface — then the answer comes from what you observed, not what you expected.

activities.title: Spot the test: a primer before you build one
feedback: When the child names the question and the one changed thing: 'That's the thing being tested — now let's go change one and watch it yourself.'
If the child treats the scene as the whole test: 'This shows what a test looks like; the real test is when you change something and see the result.'
activities.rationale: A pre-authored tap-to-reveal scene can introduce what a test looks like and the question→answer idea. Its observable limit is that the child cannot change a variable or generate a result, so it works as a primer that leads into an enacted test rather than as the main experience.
learnerActions: Explore a test set-up by revealing its parts, e.g. tap the ramp to see how high it is, tap the car to see how far it went.
Name what the test is trying to find out (its question) and what single thing is being changed.
Then move on to running your own test, where YOU change the one thing and generate the result.
activities.intendedInsight: A test has a question, one thing that changes, and a result you watch — and a real test means you change it yourself and see what happens.

activities.title: Plan-a-test talk with a science friend
feedback: If a plan changes several things: 'Pick just one thing to change — what will the rest stay as?'
After the test: 'Did the result match your guess, or surprise you? What does it tell us?'
activities.rationale: Conversation can model the plan→observe→answer loop and surface the prediction, but talk alone does not elicit the hands-on running and observing this PROCEDURAL objective requires, so at 5–7 it must be paired with a test the child actually runs and observes — real or on-screen — matching this activity's own steps. Use predict–do–observe so results can surprise and inform the child.
learnerActions: Before testing, talk through a plan: 'What one thing will you change? What will you keep the same? What will you watch?'
Run the real or on-screen test, then talk about the result: 'What did you see? So what is your answer?'
activities.intendedInsight: Planning out loud helps you pick the one thing to change and decide what to watch, so your result can actually answer the question.

activities.title: Check the loop (quick review)
feedback: For a 'changed too many things' option: 'If you change two things you won't know which one caused the result.'
When steps are ordered correctly: 'Question first, then test, then watch, then answer — that's the loop.'
activities.rationale: A short, pictorial review can confirm the child recognises the loop and the fair-test idea, including a 'changed too many things' option. Its observable limit is that it does not elicit the independent doing-and-observing, so keep it as a check around enacted tests rather than the teaching itself.
learnerActions: Answer a few pictorial checks: 'What should you change to test this?'
Put the steps in order: question → test → observe → answer.
Read an answer off a described result: given what happened, say which thing won.
activities.intendedInsight: A good test changes one thing, watches the result, and uses that result to answer the question.

constraints: Core learning requires an enacted test the child actually runs and observes (real ramps/materials or an on-screen bench where they change the variable and generate a result); recognition or tap-to-reveal scenes are scaffolds, not substitutes — this follows the PROCEDURAL 'perform simple tests' objective.
Start from a real question the child cares about so the test has an obvious purpose, and name each step: question → test → observe → 'so my answer is…'.
Keep tests concrete so cause and result are directly visible; keep text low and use audio prompts for this age.
Insist the answer comes from what was OBSERVED, not from prior belief or whether it matched the prediction.
Tap-to-reveal scenes and conversation are primers/support; a short review can confirm recognition of the loop but does not by itself elicit the independent doing and observing.

A screen bench and real materials offer different experiences; neither is claimed as universally necessary. A 3D set-up may add physicality where spatial layout is central but is not required to grasp 'change one thing, watch what happens'.
Address the misconception that one run is enough by offering the chance to repeat and check ('should we try it again?'), while allowing that a first simple-test version may legitimately run once.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Legacy entries framed 2D interactive as 'ideal' and other media as lesser; comparative-efficacy and necessity claims (e.g. 'talk without doing can't carry it', 'a scored quiz can't teach') have been softened to scoped observable affordances/limits, as catalog ratings do not establish them.

Claims that the objective 'requires physically enacted' tests were softened to 'enacted (real or on-screen) and observed' to stay consistent with the recommended on-screen bench and the activity steps.
The 'soft lock' that blocks changing more than one thing is kept as an optional example mechanism and prompt, not a mandatory feature.

Pedagogy lists repeating/checking a test as important; included as a constraint and probe, with the caveat that the first simple-test version may legitimately run once — balance repetition against young children's attention.

In the three-surface activity the car should be RELEASED rather than pushed; 'keeping the push the same' was removed to avoid implying a push, keeping the controlled-variable method consistent across action, insight and feedback.

probeDeeper: Did each surface get a fair go? What did you keep the same each time?
What did you see that tells you which one won?
If I pushed the car harder on the carpet, would that be a fair way to find out? Why not?
How could we be really sure — should we try it again?
assess.correctAnswer: The child releases the same car from the same place on the same ramp onto each surface in turn (changing only the surface), watches and describes how far the car goes each time, and answers the question from what they saw — for example, 'the smooth wood, because the car rolled furthest on it every time.'

errorPatterns.pattern: Uncontrolled comparison: gives the car a harder push, or a different starting height, on the surface they want to win — 'I helped it go on the wood'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'did each surface get a fair go? what did you change?' Model releasing (not pushing) from the same spot each time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching the set-up: the child varies the push or start point between surfaces without noticing it makes the comparison unfair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers from expectation, not observation: states the surface they predicted would win even when the car actually rolled furthest on a different one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back and look together: 'show me which one really went furthest' — tie the answer to the observed result.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A mismatch between what the child says won and what actually happened in front of them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes without concluding: narrates the fun ('it went really fast!') but never answers which surface lets it roll furthest.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the link: 'so, which surface lets the car roll the furthest?' — prompt them to use the result to answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's closing statement reports events but doesn't address the original question.

responseLevels.gap: Changes several things at once or pushes the car differently each time; states an answer that doesn't match what happened, or just describes the activity without answering.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a genuine comparison changing only the surface, observes and describes each outcome, and answers the question directly from the evidence — 'the wood, because it went furthest every time.'
responseLevels.partial: Runs a roughly fair comparison and describes each result, but needs prompting to keep everything else the same, or to connect the observation to the actual question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three ramp surfaces — carpet, smooth wood, and bubble wrap — a toy car, and a ramp. We want to find out which surface lets the car roll the furthest. Set it up and try it, then tell me which surface won and how you know. I'll watch while you do it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who runs a genuine comparison — same car, same start, only the surface changed — and reads the answer off what happened, from one who gives the car an extra push on a favourite surface, starts it from different heights, or states the answer they expected rather than what they saw. These show in the doing, not in a verbal account.
